{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "A's demand evidence is stronger. It has four sourced first-person quotes with specific prices people actually paid and resented ($8→$34/mo, $79/mo, $15/mo, $20/mo). That shows existing willingness to pay that a cheaper entrant could capture. B has only two Reddit items, one of which is a thread title.",
    "B's own brief says a new entrant is 'effectively selling against $0': OneUptime offers an unlimited free public status page, and StillOnline already holds the $9/mo indie and agent niche. That directly threatens a paying customer within 90 days. A's competitors also have free tiers, but A's quotes show users paying for monitoring and actively looking for cheaper paid alternatives.",
    "A's acquisition channels have more category-specific sourcing: Instatus's Product Hunt result (559 upvotes) and an SEO case study. B's CAC figures ($205 organic vs. $341 paid) are generic SaaS-wide statistics. B also notes that Product Hunt needs a pre-existing audience to convert.",
    "B's best proof point undercuts itself. Its brief describes Instatus as growing only about $500/mo in MRR after years, which implies slow compounding that suits long-run SEO more than a 90-day first sale.",
    "A carries real risks, and they temper this pick. It needs reliability and multi-region infrastructure, which is a harder build for one person than B's manually updated page. It also faces at least five fresh clones pushing prices toward $9/mo. Some of its revenue proof is weak: Hyperping's ~$15K MRR has no source, and the $40K Instatus figure links only to a pricing page."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's pricing-pain demand signal is a Reddit thread title, 'Why does the market leader charge $399/month for a page you update manually?'. It is a rhetorical question, not a buyer saying they pay, switched, or would pay a new vendor. B's other demand quote only supports having a status page in general, not paying for one. So B's paid-demand case rests on a single post title.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. Both briefs describe the category as saturated, and they overlap heavily: the same competitors, and Instatus as proof in both. The two briefs also cite conflicting Instatus MRR figures (~$40K reported in A vs. ~$10K sourced in B). The deciding factor is A's richer, sourced evidence of people paying for this. A's reliability burden and clone-driven price compression could easily erase that edge."
}
